      Foundations
      What is Asset-Liability Management?

      Asset-Liability Management, or ALM, is the discipline through which banks manage the structure, risks, and profitability of their balance sheet. Every bank has an ALM function because banking is fundamentally a leveraged balance sheet business: unlike most companies, which operate with a relatively balanced mix of equity and liabilities, banks deliberately keep capital low and the funding side of the balance sheet relies heavily on deposits, wholesale funding, and other liabilities, which are used to generate income from loans, securities, and other assets.

      The importance of ALM became especially visible after the failures and stress events involving Silicon Valley Bank, Credit Suisse, and other European banking stress events in 2023, where weaknesses in liquidity, interest rate risk management, and balance sheet positioning translated rapidly into banking crises.

      A weak ALM strategy will create significant costs for banks: drag in returns, inefficient use of the balance sheet, poor pricing decisions, suboptimal capital allocation, and a balance sheet that may comply with banking regulation but fails to maximize profitability.

      Each constraint — IRRBB, liquidity, capital — is managed in isolation, by different teams, using different models, with different objectives. IRRBB manages EVS. The capital team manages CET1. Treasury manages LCR. FP&A manages NIM. Nobody is solving the joint problem — but they are all looking at the same balance sheet.
      Liquidity
      Liquidity — Regulatory Framework

      Under Basel III, banks are required to maintain minimum liquidity standards designed to ensure they can survive periods of market disruption and deposit or funding stress. These requirements were introduced as part of the post-2008 Global Financial Crisis reform agenda, when regulators recognized that capital strength alone was not enough if a bank could not meet its short-term obligations.

      Basel III introduced two core liquidity ratios: the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) and the Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR). The LCR is a short-term liquidity metric designed to ensure that banks hold enough high-quality liquid assets to survive a 30-day stress scenario, while the NSFR is a longer-term structural funding metric designed to ensure that banks fund their assets and activities with a sufficiently stable funding profile over a one-year horizon.

      Liquidity Coverage Ratio — LCR

      The Liquidity Coverage Ratio measures whether a bank has enough High-Quality Liquid Assets (HQLA) to cover its expected net cash outflows over a 30-day stress period. HQLA generally includes assets that can be converted into cash quickly and reliably, even during periods of market stress — such as cash, central bank reserves, and certain high-quality government or marketable securities.

      The purpose of the LCR is to promote short-term resilience by ensuring that a bank can withstand a severe but plausible liquidity shock without immediately relying on external funding markets.

      Formula — LCR
      LCR  =  Stock of High-Quality Liquid Assets (HQLA) Total Net Cash Outflows over the next 30 calendar days  ≥  100%
      In simple terms: a bank should hold at least enough liquid resources to cover its projected net liquidity outflows during a 30-day stress event.
      Net Stable Funding Ratio — NSFR

      The Net Stable Funding Ratio measures whether a bank's assets and off-balance-sheet exposures are funded with a sufficiently stable mix of capital and liabilities. Unlike the LCR, which focuses on short-term liquidity survival, the NSFR focuses on the structural stability of the balance sheet over a longer horizon — typically one year.

      The ratio compares a bank's Available Stable Funding (ASF) — which comes from capital and liabilities considered reliable — against its Required Stable Funding (RSF) — which depends on the liquidity characteristics and maturity profile of the bank's assets and off-balance-sheet exposures.

      Formula — NSFR
      NSFR  =  Available Stable Funding (ASF) Required Stable Funding (RSF)  ≥  100%
      In simple terms: stable funding profile — long-term or less-liquid assets should not be excessively funded by short-term or unstable liabilities.
      Internal Liquidity Management

      On top of regulatory requirements such as the LCR and NSFR, banks also maintain internal liquidity stress testing frameworks. These internal models assess whether the bank has enough liquidity resources under stress conditions that may be more specific, severe, or institutionally relevant than standardised regulatory metrics.

      Typically, banks begin with today's balance sheet and apply internally defined stress assumptions to estimate how deposits, wholesale funding, loan commitments, secured funding, derivatives, and other balance sheet items may behave during a financial crisis. These assumptions often include both idiosyncratic stress (a bank-specific confidence event) and market-wide stress (a broader liquidity crisis).

      Through historical analysis, statistical models, regressions, behavioural assumptions, and expert judgment, banks estimate appropriate runoff rates and inflow assumptions for different categories of assets and liabilities. The objective is to understand what the balance sheet would look like if a severe liquidity event occurred today.

      To be considered resilient, banks typically need to remain above predefined internal liquidity limits, triggers, or survival horizons established by management and approved through the bank's risk appetite framework.

      This process allows banks to determine whether they have a liquidity surplus or deficit under stress — performed across both short-term horizons (typically 30 days) and longer-term horizons, depending on the institution's liquidity risk appetite and internal governance framework.

      The practitioner
      behind the Compass.
      Making rigorous ALM knowledge open to every practitioner — building in public since 2026.

      Daniel Morales Chavez is a Treasury and Asset-Liability Management professional with around twelve years of experience across global banking and Fortune 500 institutions, spanning interest rate risk in the banking book, liquidity risk, balance sheet management, behavioural deposit modelling, and ALCO governance under Treasury and Finance functions such as FP&A, Controlling, Accounting and Taxes.

      He is a CFA Charterholder and a member of the Hong Kong Treasury Management Association, with deep expertise in regulatory frameworks including Basel III and the HKMA Supervisory Policy Manuals in IRRBB and liquidity practice.

      The ALM Compass is his independent initiative to build an open knowledge hub he wished existed when he entered the field — and free everywhere.

      HSBC Hong Kong · FY2025 · Slide 1 of 6
      HSBC HK — FY2025 Snapshot
      Balance Sheet
      • Total Assets: HK$11.7tn (+6.7% YoY)
      • NII: HK$128.4bn (+9.2% YoY)
      • NIM: 1.68% (1.63% in 2024)
      Ratios
      • CET1 (HKMA): 19.1% (16.3% in 2024)
      • ROTE: 16.9% (18.2% in 2024)
      • Advances/Deposits: 51.3% (53.2% in 2024)
      HSBC Hong Kong · Capital · Slide 2 of 6
      A Capital Surplus Story

      CET1 climbed to 19.1% — roughly 450bps above the Group target. Two forces drove it: RWAs fell HK$209bn (−6.6%) on Basel III reform, while equity grew.

      Idle capital is a structural drag on RoTE. A bank holding capital well above target is, in effect, leaving return on equity unrealised. The strategic question: deploy, distribute, or hold?
      HSBC Hong Kong · Liquidity · Slide 3 of 6
      The Deployment Gap

      The advances-to-deposits ratio fell to 51.3%. Deposits grew +8.1% while loans grew only +4.3% — the gap is widening.

      That leaves an estimated HK$3.6tn sub-deployed — funding raised but not lent out, sitting in lower-yielding assets.

      A low A/D ratio is safe but expensive. The question is whether deposit pricing is capturing the optimal balance between funding cost and balance sheet deployment.
      HSBC Hong Kong · Capital · Slide 4 of 6
      The Output Floor Risk

      From January 2025, the Basel III output floor began phasing in. HSBC HK runs advanced IRB for the majority of its credit risk — exactly the portfolios most exposed to floor-driven RWA inflation.

      RWA inflation accelerates late in the phase-in period, making asset-mix steering a capital efficiency priority over the coming years.

      HSBC Hong Kong · Earnings · Slide 5 of 6
      The RoTE Drag

      RoTE fell to 16.9% from 18.2%. Two drags explain most of it:

      • A HK$17.2bn one-off (BoCom dilution and impairment)
      • An equity base up +4.1%, diluting the denominator

      Strip out the one-off and the underlying franchise remains highly profitable — but the growing capital base is the structural question.

      HSBC Hong Kong · Summary · Slide 6 of 6
      Key Takeaways
      • Strong capital position — CET1 ~450bps above target
      • Widening deployment gap — A/D at 51.3%, HK$3.6tn sub-deployed
      • Output floor will pressure IRB RWAs through the phase-in
      • The strategic tension: deploy surplus capital, or return it
      Source: HSBC Annual Report and Accounts 2025 (HKMA). Independent analysis — not investment advice.
      Morgan Stanley Bank Asia · FY2025 · Slide 1 of 6
      MSBAL — FY2025 Snapshot
      Balance Sheet
      • Total Assets: $9.4bn (+10.5% YoY)
      • Loans: $5.8bn (+27% YoY)
      • Deposits: $6.9bn (+12.6% YoY)
      Ratios
      • CET1: 44% (~$1.2bn excess)
      • LMR: 61% (was 77%, min 25%)
      • CFR: 135% (was 255%, min 75%)
      Morgan Stanley Bank Asia · Liquidity · Slide 2 of 6
      Growth Compressing Liquidity

      Loans grew a striking +27% in one year. The liquidity ratios show the cost: LMR halved from 77% to 61%, and CFR collapsed from 255% to 135%.

      Both ratios remain comfortably above minimums (25% and 75%), but the trajectory is steep. Rapid asset growth is consuming the liquidity buffer that was previously very large.
      Morgan Stanley Bank Asia · Funding · Slide 3 of 6
      New Intercompany Funding

      A new $0.85bn intercompany deposit with maturity beyond 12 months appeared — "deposits to other MS Group undertakings."

      The likely driver: shoring up the CFR (Core Funding Ratio) as loan growth consumes stable funding. Long-dated intercompany funding is a classic lever to defend a structural funding ratio.

      Morgan Stanley Bank Asia · Capital · Slide 4 of 6
      A 44% CET1 Ratio

      CET1 stands at 44% — roughly $1.2bn of excess capital — with no dividends paid.

      For a subsidiary growing loans at 27%, holding capital is partly prudent (supporting growth) and partly a capital optimisation opportunity. The trade-off between retained flexibility and upstreamed return is the open question.
      Morgan Stanley Bank Asia · IRRBB · Slide 5 of 6
      UHNW Deposit Behaviour

      The bank holds roughly $6bn of UHNW deposits, of which ~$2.8bn (45%) are CASA — current and savings accounts.

      If NMD models follow the HKMA IR-1 prescribed treatment with no behavioural deviation, CASA may default to overnight. For sticky UHNW relationships, that could be too conservative — understating the true behavioural duration and the EVS position.

      Morgan Stanley Bank Asia · Summary · Slide 6 of 6
      Key Takeaways
      • Aggressive loan growth (+27%) compressing liquidity ratios
      • New long-dated intercompany funding defending CFR
      • 44% CET1 — large excess, no distribution
      • UHNW CASA may justify behavioural NMD modelling beyond prescribed
      Source: MSBAL Annual Report 2025 (HKMA). Independent analysis — not investment advice.
      J.P. Morgan Private Bank HK · FY2025 · Slide 1 of 5
      JPM Private Bank — FY2025 Snapshot
      HK Branch (HKMA)
      • Operating Income: HK$13.5bn (+6.3%)
      • Profit Before Tax: HK$3.9bn (+4.6%)
      • Total Assets: HK$171.6bn
      Revenue Mix
      • Net Fees & Commission: HK$11.4bn (+17%)
      • Interest Income: fell HK$1.2bn (−21%)
      J.P. Morgan Private Bank HK · Earnings · Slide 2 of 5
      A Fee-Driven Engine

      The revenue story is a clear rotation: interest income fell HK$1.2bn (−21%) as rates moved, while fees rose HK$1.7bn (+17%).

      Unlike a traditional balance sheet bank, the private bank's P&L is driven by AUM-linked fees, not net interest margin. The growth engine is assets under management and net new money — not the loan book.
      J.P. Morgan Private Bank HK · Global Context · Slide 3 of 5
      The AWM Division

      The HK branch sits within JPM's global Asset & Wealth Management division (FY2025):

      • Revenue: USD $24bn
      • AUM: USD $4.8tn (+18% YoY)
      • ROE: 40%
      • Ranked #1 Private Bank globally
      J.P. Morgan Private Bank HK · Treasury Lens · Slide 4 of 5
      What an FP&A Desk Tracks

      For a fee-driven private bank, the treasury and FP&A focus shifts away from NIM toward:

      • AUM-linked revenue — the primary income driver
      • Net new money — the leading indicator of future fees
      • Deposit behaviour — UHNW client balances as cheap funding
      J.P. Morgan Private Bank HK · Summary · Slide 5 of 5
      Key Takeaways
      • Fee income (+17%) now the dominant P&L driver, not NII
      • Interest income fell 21% as the rate cycle turned
      • Backed by a global AWM franchise — $4.8tn AUM, 40% ROE
      • The metric that matters: AUM growth and net new money
      Source: JPM HK Branch HKMA Disclosure FY2025 · JPMorgan Chase 4Q25 Earnings · AWM Letter 2025. Independent analysis — not investment advice.

      Liquidity · Slide 1 of 8
      Why Liquidity Matters

      Under Basel III, banks must hold minimum liquidity to survive market disruption and funding stress. Capital strength alone is not enough — a solvent bank can still fail if it cannot meet short-term obligations.

      Two regulatory ratios anchor the framework:

      • LCR — short-term resilience over a 30-day stress horizon
      • NSFR — structural funding stability over a one-year horizon
      The 2023 failures of Silicon Valley Bank and Credit Suisse were fundamentally liquidity events — deposit flight outpaced the banks’ ability to raise cash, even where capital looked adequate.
      Liquidity · Slide 2 of 8
      What the Regulation Requires
      • LCR ≥ 100% — enough High-Quality Liquid Assets (HQLA) to cover 30-day net stressed outflows
      • NSFR ≥ 100% — Available Stable Funding must cover Required Stable Funding
      • Internal stress tests — beyond the regulatory minimums, banks run their own scenarios under the risk appetite framework

      Regulators expect banks to remain above these thresholds at all times, with management buffers on top. In Hong Kong, the HKMA sets local implementation through the Banking (Liquidity) Rules and SPM module LM-2.

      Liquidity · Slide 3 of 8
      Key Metrics & Formulas
      LCR = Stock of HQLA ÷ Net Cash Outflows (30 days) ≥ 100%
      Measures short-term survival under a severe but plausible 30-day stress.
      NSFR = Available Stable Funding ÷ Required Stable Funding ≥ 100%
      Measures whether long-term assets are funded by stable sources over one year.
      Liquidity · Slide 4 of 8
      Sources of Information
      Global
      • BCBS — LCR standard (BCBS238)
      • BCBS — NSFR standard (d295)
      Hong Kong
      • HKMA SPM LM-2
      • Banking (Liquidity) Rules
      • HKMA return MA(BS)1E

      For internal frameworks, the bank’s own ILAAP (Internal Liquidity Adequacy Assessment Process) documents assumptions, runoff rates, and survival horizons.

      Liquidity · Slide 5 of 8
      Worked Example — LCR

      A bank holds USD 16bn HQLA (cash, reserves, govt bonds). Under a 30-day stress it projects:

      • Deposit outflows: USD 18bn
      • Wholesale runoff: USD 4bn
      • Inflows (capped at 75%): USD 7bn
      Net outflows = 22 − 7 = USD 15bn
      LCR = 16 ÷ 15 = 106.7%
      Above 100% — compliant, but only a 6.7% buffer. Most banks target 120%+ internally.
      Liquidity · Slide 6 of 8
      Levers to Improve LCR
      • Increase HQLA — rotate non-HQLA assets into govt bonds or central bank reserves (raises numerator)
      • Lengthen funding — replace <30-day wholesale funding with term funding beyond the horizon (lowers outflows)
      • Grow stable deposits — retail and operational deposits carry lower runoff factors than wholesale
      • Reduce undrawn commitments — lower committed facilities reduce contingent outflows
      Each lever has a cost: HQLA earns low yield, term funding is more expensive. The art of ALM is meeting the ratio at the lowest drag on net interest margin.
      Liquidity · Slide 7 of 8
      Levers to Improve NSFR
      • Extend liability tenor — longer-dated funding earns higher ASF factors
      • Grow capital & stable retail deposits — both are high-ASF sources
      • Shorten or reduce illiquid assets — lower RSF requirement
      • Reduce encumbrance — encumbered assets attract higher RSF factors

      NSFR and LCR levers often align — lengthening funding helps both — but not always. Always model the joint effect.

      Liquidity · Slide 8 of 8
      Key Takeaways
      • LCR protects the 30-day horizon; NSFR protects the 1-year structural profile
      • Both must stay ≥ 100%; banks hold internal buffers above
      • Internal stress testing (ILAAP) goes beyond regulatory minimums
      • Every lever trades liquidity safety against margin — optimisation, not maximisation, is the goal
      Next: explore the Capital and IRRBB trainings to see how the three pillars interact on a single balance sheet.
